results.summary: This analog test chip evaluates mismatch in a simple CMOS beta multiplier 1uA current source. It contains eight identical cells in one orientation and eight rotated 90 degrees, with all current outputs wired together to a single analog pin. Individual cells can be disabled via digital input pins to measure the current contributed by each cell. A silicon test report confirms the current source is functional, with measured currents around 0.4-0.9 uA per cell, though no external hardware is required.

This hardware module converts Unicode code points between UTF-8, UTF-16, and UTF-32 encodings. It detects and signals errors such as overlong encodings, out-of-range code points, and invalid byte sequences, with an option to disable range checking for the original UTF-8 specification. The design is intended to be used by any device that processes Unicode text, and it provides dedicated output pins for status signals like READY, ERROR, and various error types. Testing is supported by a comprehensive test set included in the project's test.py file, covering many edge cases.

This ALU implements the five operators of the INTERCAL programming language, including unary AND/OR/XOR, interleave, and select, operating on 32-bit registers. It is controlled via address, selector, and write/read enable pins, with data transferred through bidirectional and dedicated output pins. The design is primarily educational and can be tested using example calculations from the INTERCAL manual, as included in its test suite. External hardware such as a microcontroller is recommended for driving inputs and reading outputs, as the chip itself has no display or interface.

The Styler chip manipulates a 16x16 character glyph bitmap based on text mode attributes such as bold, italic, underline, blink, and cursor display. It contains registers for scanline, control, bitmap, and attributes, and supports operations like double width/height, mirroring, and various text decorations. The chip is intended to be part of a larger text mode video display system, and it is accessed through an address bus and bidirectional data pins. Testing details have not been defined, but the register layout and usage steps are thoroughly documented.

This project is a universal binary-to-segment decoder that includes four modules: a BCD to 7-segment decoder, an ASCII to 7-segment decoder, a dual BCD to Cistercian numeral decoder, and a BCV to Kaktovik numeral decoder. Each module supports various customization options for digit appearance, and the design is intended to drive segmented displays. Testing is extensive, with a dedicated test directory for each module, and external hardware includes standard 7-segment displays for BCD/ASCII modes and custom segmented displays for Cistercian and Kaktovik modes. The design is notable for supporting unusual numeral systems like Cistercian and Kaktovik, which are rarely implemented in hardware.

This design displays a 480x480 pixel Tiny Tapeout logo on a VGA monitor, using compressed data and dithered colors to fit into a single tile. It generates standard VGA signals including red, green, blue, horizontal sync, and vertical sync. The design requires an external VGA PMOD and a VGA monitor for operation, and it has been tested successfully by a silicon tester who confirmed the video works as expected. Notable features include the large resolution crammed into a small area and the use of dithering for color effects.

This design is an audio/visual demo that generates VGA video and PWM audio outputs, forming an 8-part megademo. It uses eight PWM audio pins and standard VGA pins for red, green, blue, and sync signals. The demo requires external hardware: a VGA PMOD and audio output hardware. Silicon tests report that both audio and video work as expected, and one tester described it as a very nice demo with polished graphics and audio.

This project implements a fuzzy logic system that estimates a risk value based on rainfall and soil moisture inputs. It uses triangular membership functions to evaluate inputs as low, medium, or high, and applies three fuzzy rules to compute a weighted average risk output. The design requires external hardware: eight switches for sensor inputs, one switch for sensor selection, and an 8-bit LED display for the risk output. Testing involves feeding different sensor data and verifying the expected risk levels (high, low, medium).

This design implements a ring oscillator operating in the GHz range, with a divider to produce an observable output frequency around 20 MHz. It includes a test/debug mode and an enable pin to control the oscillator. Testing requires an oscilloscope, power supply, and function generator, and the documentation suggests monitoring supply current to verify functionality. A silicon test report indicates the design is broken: no output was observed, and debug outputs were not accessible due to pin configuration issues.

This is a quick test of a SKY130 ROM compiler, implementing a small ROM array with wordline and bitline controls. It supports two read methods: pullup and precharge, as described in the silicon test reports. The design has minimal documentation, with sections marked as FIXME, so its intended usage and requirements are unclear. Silicon tests indicate it works: the author successfully read the test array using both methods, though the precharge data decays in about 2 ms and always decays to 0x11 on that chip.
